title: The solver: what a miss types
goal: Know what keymux types for a stroke or `+` run the dictionary does not have, how the solver works that out, what it costs to type loosely, and the plain read-back it falls back on.

blocks.x: What it is

lyk ships a keymux plugin, **the solver** (`05-lyk-solver.rs`, with its lexicon in `05-lyk-solver.bin` beside it). keymux asks it about anything every dictionary missed: a single stroke, or a `+` run, which is always one word. It answers with the word (or the word and its suffixes) those strokes most likely mean, read from the same tables the generator writes with. Nothing has to be a dictionary entry for it to type: an outline the generator never listed still types its word when its keys say that word's sounds.

items: **It answers again on every stroke.** A `+` run has no word boundary inside it, so keymux hands the solver the whole run after each new stroke and the new answer replaces the old one. A word can read as something else halfway through (`KOPL/+PU` reads *champa*) and settles on the right one when the run is done (`KOPL/+PU/+TER` *computer*).
**It never overrides the dictionary.** keymux asks the dictionary files first; the solver only sees what none of them has.

**It is what makes `+` a join key.** keymux itself gives no key a meaning; the solver's `joins` answer is what tells keymux that a `+` stroke continues the word before it and is never a word of its own.
**Spelling mode is unchanged.** A run that starts with `~` is read one letter a stroke from `rules/spelling.toml` ([spelling mode](#/ref/spelling-mode)).

blocks.x: How it reads a run
1. Every reading of every stroke
Each stroke is read back into every run of sounds its keys can write, not just one:

items: **Each bank, every way it splits into chords** of the onset and coda tables (`PHR` is M R or P L; `-PBLG` is JH, or N JH, or the keys one at a time), up to 48 ways a bank. Bigger chords are tried first.
**The vowel keys as any vowel they write**: as heard (`O` is the vowel of *hot*), or as a spelling the rules give them (`O` is also the *o* of *control*, `AE` the *ea* of *mean*).

**A vowel and the consonant after it together** where the rules have that chord (`AR`, `OPBG`, `AEUR`), and a vowel whose own chord reaches into the right hand (`UR` is the ER of *turn*, `EUR` the *ir* of *bird*). A vowel key alone never stands for such a vowel.

**A prefix chord, on a run's first stroke only**: the keys of a prefix entry of `rules/plover.toml` read as the prefix's sounds before the rest of the onset (`KP` is *ex-*: `KPEL` *excel*, `KPOT/+EUBG` *exotic*; also `STK` *dis-*, `TPHR` *inter-*, `TKPHR` *under-*, `SR` *over-*, `SPH` *mis-*, `TPH` *un-*). Costs 1. The keys keep their plain reading too.
**The star** as part of a chord (`*T` is TH) or, when nothing claims it, as the homophone marker, which writes no sound.

**A stroke of the star alone (`+*`) that ends a run steps one word down**: the run without it reads as its best word, and each `+*` after it takes the next one. `TP/+EUT` is *fight*, `TP/+EUT/+*` *fit*; `*T/+U/+-PL` is *them*, `+*` *thumb*, a second `+*` *time*. A `+*` inside a run is the marker: it costs 1 and reads as nothing.
**The consonants after the vowel in every order**, three or fewer: the keys are in steno order, the sounds need not be (`PWERT` is *better*).
**A chord that shares the vowel's `R` key** (`V.rv` `-FRB`, `CH.rch` `-FRPB`) is also that R and its consonant, free: `-S/+TAFRBZ` is *starves*, `-BG/+AFRBD` *carved*.

**A left-hand stroke alone, after the first, is the word's next consonants in any order, free**: the left bank can only strike them in steno order (`KUR/+STKPWHR` is *curls*, its L Z struck Z then L).

Of a stroke's readings, the 40 cheapest within 4 of the best are tried; of equal cost, those with the fewest sounds first (`STKPWHR` as Z L before J DH P). A first stroke's 3 best readings with a prefix chord in it are tried as well, cap or not (`STKERT/+AEU/+-GS` *dissertation*, `STPHAOUT/+UBL` *unsuitable*).

blocks.x: 2. Matched against every word

The lexicon is every word among the 100,000 commonest that has a pronunciation (the generator's own vocabulary), each written into one tree twice: by its pronunciation, and by a reading of its spelling (each letter a sound, a vowel letter short, long or weak, as the generator's spelled backups read it). The run's sounds are matched along that tree, and every way they differ from a word costs something:

head: The run versus the word
Cost
rows: a sound that matches
a vowel struck as the word spells it, not as it is heard (`O` for the *o* of *control*); a single vowel letter only for a vowel spelled with that letter alone (*said*'s *ai* is not an `EU`)
a vowel struck as a letter the word does not spell it with
a vowel struck as a different vowel
`-R` for the vowel ER (`PHART`, *mat-er-nal*)
a consonant read as its twin (P B, T D, K G, F V, TH DH, S Z, SH ZH, CH JH, N NG, M N)
a chord whose sound the rules tie to a spelling (`-D` as the T of *-ed*, `-G` as *-ing*)
two consonants of one stroke in the other order: `R` or `L` / any other
the star as the homophone marker

a sound of the word the run skipped: a reduced vowel (unstressed `AH`, `IH`, `ER`) / any other unstressed or a secondary-stressed vowel / a stressed vowel / `HH` or the `Y` glide / any other consonant
the word's last vowel skipped when it is not a reduced one (the *-ly* of *probably*, the *-y* of its spelling): on top of the above
the consonant the word ends on skipped (*problem*'s M, so `PRO/+-BL` is *probably*, 9, not *problem*, 10): on top of the above
a sound in the run the word does not have
the word reached by its spelling rather than its sounds
the same, with the word's silent final *e* struck as an *e* (`TKA/+-PB/+SE` *dance*, not *dancer*; `PW/+EU/+K/+E` *bike*)
the word's rarity: half a point for every doubling of its rank (*the* 0, rank 1,000 about 5, rank 50,000 about 8)
0 to 8

items: At most three sounds of a word in a row are skipped, and a word starts with at most one skipped sound, a weak one (the *a-* of *about*).

**A tie goes to the commoner word.** Rarity is rounded to whole points, so homophones often cost the same: `AEU/+T` is *eight*, not *ate*; `TA/+P` *tape*, not *tap*; `PWO/+-R/+-G` *boring* (*bore* + *-ing*), not *baring*.
**An abbreviation said in full** (*tv* also said *television*: more sounds than twice its letters plus one) is not matched by those sounds: they type the full word.

**Every stroke is used.** A stroke of a run must match at least one sound of the word it is read into (or be a suffix chord or a known outline): a stroke you strike is never explained away as sounds the word does not have. Sounds can be doubled or missing; the order is kept (only the consonants of one stroke may swap, as above).
The cheapest reading wins. Two words that read the same go to the commoner one: a homophone struck with no spelling cue types the commoner word.

blocks.x: 3. Pieces
A run can be read as several pieces, each a word, a suffix or a known outline, joined with no space:

head: Piece
When
Cost
rows: a word of the lexicon
anywhere, on whole strokes
as above, plus 10 for every piece after the first
a suffix chord ([suffix table](#/ref/suffixes), one or two strokes)
any stroke after the first that carries `+`, unconditionally; the stroke may still be read as sounds instead
a hard suffix: the chord with `*` added to its first stroke (`+*D`, the suffix sheet's own entry)
the same, and the stroke is never read as sounds: it is the suffix
a known outline: the exact outline of any entry of the words, short, alternates or extras files, or one the rules teach a word (`explain`'s "ours", two strokes or more: `WAUT/+-R` *water*)
on whole strokes; the first piece, or a later one (+2)
the word's rarity, plus 10 after the first piece
a misstroke: a stroke one key more or one key fewer than a known one-stroke outline
one stroke, anywhere a known outline could be
5, plus the same as a known outline

items: **A known outline can carry on into a longer word.** After a known outline, the strokes that follow may go on with the same word's sounds instead of starting a new piece: `AUGS` is *audition*, so `AUGS/+AOEUPBG` reads *auditioning*, priced as *auditioning* plus 1. It also carries on into any longer word **spelled** from it, however that word says those letters, when the outline's word is 3 letters or more and the longer word goes on with a vowel letter: `KWEULD` is *liquid*, so `KWEULD/+ARB/+UPB` reads *liquidation* (said *liquad-*), and *inc* goes on into *incorporate*. At most 8 such places per outline, its own word's sounds first, then the most common longer words.

**An outline the rules teach a word, struck whole, is that word, before anything else**: `WAUT/+-R` is *water*, never *wait* + *-er*. The plugin carries every lexicon word's taught outlines (its outline and its homophone variant), the ones the lessons have you strike syllable by syllable; an outline a dictionary entry holds stays that entry's, and two words taught the same outline give it to the commoner (*theater* over *theatre*).

**Then a word you know plus ending chords, when they spell a real word, is that word.** `PROB/+-BL` is *prob* + *-able*: *probable*, whatever the sounds might also say. When they spell no word (`PRO/+-BL`, *pro* + *able*), the run is read by its sounds (*pro-bly*: *probably*). Only an outline you struck counts, never a misstroke guess one key off it: `SKRAEPL/+-Z` is *screams*, not *cream* + *s*. Three rules, in order: a brief or a taught outline, struck whole, is its word; a known word plus endings is that word; otherwise the sounds decide.

**Pieces that spell a word are that word**, never cheaper than the pieces themselves: *part* + `+-S` is as rare as *parts*, and a rare piece does not become a common word by spelling one. *part* + `+-S` is *parts*, priced at the rarity of *parts*, not of *part*.

**Words joined that spell a real word the lexicon lacks are that word.** The plugin also carries a list of real spellings down to rank 250,000 of the frequency list (no sounds, only the spelling): `HRAOBG/+UP` is *look* + *up*, *lookup* (rank 121,405), not *lockup*. Each join costs 2 there, not 10, and the word is priced at its own rarity, never below its pieces'. Only words joined to words: a stem and suffix chords must spell a lexicon word, since the list's tail holds misspellings (*regreting*).
**Pieces that spell no word** cost 6 more: allowed, for a word the lexicon lacks, but only when nothing that is a word reads as well.
A word piece only ends at a stroke boundary; a suffix chord is always the suffix, never its bare consonants.

4. The floor: the plain read-back

When no reading costs 40 or less, plus 6 for each stroke, the solver types the run's keys read back as plain sounds instead (below): a run that sounds like no word types what its keys say, not a far-fetched word. A run longer than 24 strokes is read on its first 24, the strokes after them read back as keys and added on: none is dropped. keymux asks again on every stroke; the solver goes on from the run it read last where the two agree, so each stroke is one stroke's work however long the run (1.1 ms a stroke on average in wasm), with the same answer as reading the run afresh.
The plain read-back

Each stroke's plainest reading, its sounds spelled plainly (not real orthography: no word is on record to give one). It is what the solver types below its floor, and what `!resolve` and `!lookup` print for a miss when no solver is built.

items: A vowelless stroke reads with no invented vowel: `-T` alone reads `!t`.
A suffix chord after the first stroke reads as its suffix: `+-D` reads `!ed`, not `!d`.

Every key means something on its own and every one of the 15 non-empty vowel-key combinations is a vowel, so almost every stroke reads as something. The only stroke with no reading is one with no onset, vowel or coda once the star and join keys are set aside.

blocks.x: Where two sounds share keys, the read-back breaks the tie the same way every time (`vowel_rank` in `src/rules/mod.rs`). Bare `AO` is a three-way tie, `UH` (*book*), `UW.oo` (*moon*) and `OW.oa` (*boat*); it reads **`UW.oo`**.
No backups in keymux

`deploy` ships **no backups**. Any outline that sounds like a word is read by the solver, so keymux holds no list of the dozens of ways into each word: a word keeps its primary outline and its other entries (short forms, alternates, extras), and every other outline types whatever the solver reads it as. `build` still writes the generated backups to `out/lyk/02-lyk-backups.json`, never deployed: they are the solver's test set (`solve --eval` reads every Nth one and checks it types its word, 85% do) and the catalogue `lookup` and this site list ways into a word from. An outline whose backup word differs from what the solver reads types the solver's word.
Try it

cargo run --release -- solve KOPL/+PU/+TER          # every reading of a run, cheapest first
cargo run --release -- solve -- "-L/+AOF"           # a run that starts with a right-hand stroke
cargo run --release -- solve --eval 250              # read every 250th backup: how often is it its word?
cargo run --release -- solve --tape ~/.local/state/keymux/steno-tape.txt   # the tape's misses against what was struck next
cargo run --release -- resolve TOLT                  # what a miss types, beside its nearest entries
`!resolve` (alias `stroke`) and `!lookup` print what the outline types in quotes; for a miss that is the solver's answer, marked as a reading, when `build` has written the solver to `out/lyk`.
